items.X: Total means all six congruent square faces.
items.Z: Instantiate total cube surface area from six equal faces.
hints: What does total surface area count on a cube?
Each face is a square of side 7 cm; connect one-face area to the number of faces.
Write one expression for all congruent faces; keep the arithmetic for yourself.

representation.reason: A cube sketch adds no demand-specific reasoning value for this demonstrated revision learner.

misconception.M1: Use 4a² or a³ because the object is a cube.
misconception.M2: Ask how many square faces contribute to total surface area.
misconception.M3: Inventory physical faces first, then sum their areas.

items.X: The stated 14 cm is a diameter while 2πrh uses radius.
items.Y: Demonstrated circle diameter-radius and cylinder curved-area relations.
items.Z: Map diameter to the formula variable, then execute curved surface area.
items.W: Make the d→r mapping and complete the substitution.
hints: Which surface is requested: curved wall only, or bases too?
Check whether your chosen formula expects r or d.
Translate every given into the variables of that formula before multiplying.

representation.reason: A diameter-versus-radius cross-section helps only if that mapping is the sticking point; it must not reveal r=7 numerically.

misconception.M2: Ask the learner to label r and d on a circle.
misconception.M3: Radius is half the diameter; map givens before execution.

items.X: An open bucket has a curved wall and one base but no top disk.
items.Z: Form the sheet-area model from physically present surfaces.
items.W: Choose the correct surface sum and execute it.
hints: Before using a formula, name the actual pieces of metal sheet.
Connect 'open at the top' to whether a top circular sheet exists.
Write area as the sum of only those physical pieces, then substitute.

representation.reason: Show curved wall, bottom disk and absent top without writing the final surface sum.

misconception.M1: Use closed-cylinder total surface area or curved surface area alone.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to point to every physical sheet piece.
misconception.M3: Surface-area formulas are inventories of present surfaces, not keyword selections.

items.independent_check: Closed-cylinder area is 1100 cm²; subtract one missing top disk, 154 cm², to get 946 cm².

items.X: Vertical height is not the slant length used in cone curved surface area.
items.Y: Demonstrated Pythagoras/slant-height bridge and cone curved-area relation.
items.Z: Derive l from r and h, then use l in πrl.
items.W: Coordinate the dependency and carry out both steps.
hints: Which length actually lies along the canvas from apex to rim?
A central cross-section contains r, h and l as a right triangle.
Resolve the needed length first; only then evaluate the open cone's canvas area.

representation.reason: Axial cross-section with r=7, h=24 and l unknown plus an open-base cue; do not reveal l=25 pre-attempt.

misconception.M1: Use πrh with vertical height or add the base area.
misconception.M2: Ask which segment lies on the sloping fabric and whether the base is covered.
misconception.M3: Derive slant height from the right triangle; an open base contributes no canvas.

items.independent_check: 7-24-25 satisfies Pythagoras; π×7×25 = 550 m² using π=22/7.

items.X: The open bowl's inner surface is curved; its mouth is not a material disk.
items.Z: Distinguish curved hemisphere area from total hemisphere area.
items.W: Choose 2πr² and justify excluding the disk.
hints: Imagine touching every material point on the inside of the bowl.
At the mouth, is there material filling the circle or just an opening?
Choose the hemisphere-area expression that matches only the material interior.

representation.reason: A cross-section may show curved wall and open mouth but must not shade a nonexistent disk.

misconception.M1: Use 3πr² because 'hemisphere' triggers total surface area.
misconception.M2: Ask whether a flat disk physically exists at the mouth.
misconception.M3: Formula choice follows surface inventory; an open mouth is not a surface.

items.independent_check: Adding πr² would convert curved area to total hemisphere area; that extra term is exactly the nonexistent base disk.

items.X: The solids share an internal circular interface and the cone also needs a derived slant height.
items.Z: Coordinate derived slant height with an exposed-surface inventory across the composite solid.
items.W: Obtain l, identify only reachable exterior surfaces, and combine them without the joint.
hints: If you painted the completed toy, which surfaces could the brush actually touch?
The cone's needed side length is not 12 cm; locate the right triangle that determines it.
After finding that length, build one expression for the reachable exterior only. Test every candidate circle with 'is it visible after joining?'

representation.reason: Show assembled cone-on-hemisphere and, if useful, a ghost/exploded view of the shared interface; mark the joint internal without stating the final sum.

misconception.M1: Count one or both shared circular faces, or use 12 cm as slant height.
misconception.M2: Ask whether paint can reach the joint and which triangle contains l.
misconception.M3: Internal coincident faces contribute zero exposed area; derive l before cone curved area.

items.independent_check: Wrongly counting the hidden disk adds π(3.5)²=38.5 cm²; the correct exposed area is 214.5 cm².

items.X: Translate the paint specification into exactly two surface terms.
items.Y: Demonstrated surface inventory plus circle/cylinder area relations.
items.Z: Model painted area as outer curved wall plus outside base.
items.W: Write and execute the correct two-term expression after naming surfaces.
hints: Cross out every region the wording explicitly says is not painted.
Match each remaining physical surface to its own area relation.
Add only those remaining terms; do not introduce a top or any inside surface.

representation.reason: The wording already enumerates surfaces; a figure is only a spatial check and must not rely on color alone.

misconception.M1: Include the inside surface or a top disk.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to list painted surfaces before writing a formula.
misconception.M3: Translate condition to surface inventory to area expression.

items.independent_check: Adding one top disk would change the answer by exactly 154 cm².

items.X: Preserve order and units through full volume to 75% fill to litres.
items.Y: Demonstrated volume units and litre conversion.
items.Z: Execute rectangular-prism, percentage and conversion chain.
items.W: Perform the chain without mixing linear, area or volume conversion factors.
hints: Find the tank's full volume before applying the fill fraction.
Treat 75% as a multiplier on volume, not on one dimension.
Keep m³ through the geometry; convert the final water volume to litres.

representation.reason: A tank or fill graphic adds little reasoning value; the meaningful representation is the unit-labelled calculation chain.

misconception.M1: Apply 75% to one dimension or use an incorrect m³-to-litre factor.
misconception.M2: Ask what physical quantity 75% describes and what 1 m³ equals in litres.
misconception.M3: Percent fill acts on capacity; 1 m³=1000 L.

items.X: Identify what is conserved by 'no metal lost' and distinguish it from surface area.
items.Y: Demonstrated conservation of volume in recasting.
items.Z: Formulate V_large=n·V_small and use r³ scaling.
items.W: Choose volume as the invariant and solve for n.
hints: What quantity measures the amount of metal before and after reshaping?
For similar spheres, volume scales with the cube of radius.
Represent the recast condition as one large-sphere volume equalling n small-sphere volumes.

representation.reason: A before/after schematic may show reshaping but must not depict exactly 27 small spheres or imply the picture proves conservation.

misconception.M1: Conserve surface area or use the linear radius ratio 6/2.
misconception.M2: Ask which quantity no-metal-lost constrains and how sphere volume scales with radius.
misconception.M3: Material amount fixes volume; subdivision generally changes total boundary area.

items.independent_check: 27×2³=6³; total smaller-sphere surface area is 432π cm² versus 144π cm² originally.

items.X: Compare the formulas structurally instead of reconstructing r and h.
items.Y: Demonstrated cone/cylinder volume relations and common-factor reasoning.
items.Z: Derive the volume ratio for equal radius and height.
items.W: Establish the one-third relation and apply it to 924.
hints: Write the two formulas symbolically before inserting any number.
Mark the factor that is identical because radius and height are the same.
Form V_cone/V_cylinder; simplify the common factor, then use the given cylinder volume.

representation.reason: An SVG would not improve the decisive reasoning; the useful representation is the symbolic formula comparison.

misconception.M1: Solve for r and h separately or assume cone volume is half the cylinder.
misconception.M2: Ask which factors differ between the two formulas.
misconception.M3: With identical base radius and height, only the coefficient 1/3 differs.

clusters.construction: Name present, absent, hidden and exposed surfaces before selecting formulas.
Derive a required geometric length before applying a surface-area relation.
Use volume as capacity, a conserved invariant, and a common symbolic factor.
